summary.text: Quadratic reciprocity shows that five is a square modulo the given prime; choosing the even representative among the two roots gives an even \(x\) with \(4\le x<p\), and setting \(n=x-1\) yields \(x^2-5=pc\) with positive odd \(c<n\). Writing the continued fraction as \(P_2/P_3\), the continuant recurrence gives \(P_2=pc\), while a factorial identity and \(\gcd(c,8)=1\) force \(c\mid P_3\); if \(p\mid P_3/c\), divisibility propagates through the recurrence to \(p\mid P_n=4\), so reduction leaves numerator exactly \(p\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
R_k(n)=k-\frac{k+1}{R_{k+1}(n)}\qquad (2\leq k<n-1),
\]
with
\[
R_{n-1}(n)=(n-1)-\frac n{-4}=(n-1)+\frac n4.
\]
Thus the continued fraction in the definition of the sequence is
\[
C_n=\frac1{R_2(n)}.
\]
If the rational number \(R_2(n)\) is written in lowest terms as \(N/D\), with \(D>0\), then \(C_n=D/N\), so the reduced denominator of \(C_n\) is \(|N|\). We shall prove that for a suitable \(n\), the reduced numerator of \(R_2(n)\) is the prescribed prime \(p\).

We first establish the facts about the continued fraction that will be needed.

### 1. Integer continuants for the tails

For fixed \(n\geq3\), define integers \(P_k=P_k(n)\) backwards by
\[
P_n=4,\qquad P_{n-1}=5n-4,
\]
and, for \(2\leq k<n-1\),
\[
P_k=kP_{k+1}-(k+1)P_{k+2}. \tag{1}
\]
Then
\[
R_k(n)=\frac{P_k}{P_{k+1}} \qquad (2\leq k\leq n-1). \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, at the terminal index,
\[
R_{n-1}(n)=n-1+\frac n4=\frac{5n-4}{4}
 =\frac{P_{n-1}}{P_n}.
\]
If (2) holds at \(k+1\), then
\[
R_k(n)=k-\frac{k+1}{P_{k+1}/P_{k+2}}
=\frac{kP_{k+1}-(k+1)P_{k+2}}{P_{k+1}}
=\frac{P_k}{P_{k+1}},
\]
provided the relevant tails are nonzero. The required nonvanishing also follows from the positivity estimate below, so this backward induction is valid.

The key closed form is
\[
P_2=n^2+2n-4. \tag{3}
\]
Here is a derivation of this identity. Introduce an auxiliary integer sequence \(T_k\) by
\[
T_2=1,\qquad T_3=0,
\]
and, for \(k\geq2\),
\[
T_{k+2}=k(T_{k+1}-T_k). \tag{4}
\]
A direct induction using (1), (4), and the factorial recursion gives, for every \(2\leq k\leq n\),
\[
P_k=\frac{2P_3(k-2)+P_2T_k}{(k-1)!}. \tag{5}
\]
For completeness, (5) is immediate at \(k=2\) and \(k=3\): its right side is respectively \(P_2\) and \(2P_3/2=P_3\). If it holds at two consecutive indices \(j,j+1\), solve (1) for
\[
P_{j+2}=\frac{jP_{j+1}-P_j}{j+1}.
\]
Substitution of the two induction hypotheses, followed by use of
\(T_{j+2}=j(T_{j+1}-T_j)\), gives (5) at \(j+2\).

The auxiliary sequence also satisfies
\[
(n-3)T_n-(n-2)T_{n-1}=-(n-2)! \qquad(n\geq4). \tag{6}
\]
To see this, write \(n=d+4\). The assertion becomes
\[
(d+1)T_{d+4}-(d+2)T_{d+3}=-(d+2)!.
\]
For \(d=0\), (4) gives \(T_4=2(T_3-T_2)=-2\), so both sides equal \(-2\). If the identity holds for \(d\), then (4) gives
\[
T_{d+5}=(d+3)(T_{d+4}-T_{d+3}),
\]
and substituting this into the expression for \(d+1\) shows that it is \(d+3\) times the expression for \(d\). Its value is therefore
\(-(d+3)(d+2)!=-(d+3)!\), proving (6).

Apply (5) first with \(k=n\) and then with \(k=n-1\). Since \(P_n=4\), \(P_{n-1}=5n-4\), these equations are
\[
4(n-1)!=2P_3(n-2)+P_2T_n, \tag{7}
\]
\[
(5n-4)(n-2)!=2P_3(n-3)+P_2T_{n-1}. \tag{8}
\]
Multiply (7) by \(n-3\), multiply (8) by \(n-2\), and subtract. The terms containing \(P_3\) cancel. By (6), the right side is
\(-P_2(n-2)!\). On the other hand, using \((n-1)!=(n-1)(n-2)!\), the left side is
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(n-3)4(n-1)!-(n-2)(5n-4)(n-2)!\\
&=(n-2)!\bigl(4(n-3)(n-1)-(n-2)(5n-4)\bigr)\\
&=-(n-2)!(n^2+2n-4).
\end{aligned}
\]
Since a factorial is nonzero, cancellation proves (3) for \(n\geq4\). For \(n=3\), it follows directly from the terminal value: \(P_2=5\cdot3-4=11=3^2+2\cdot3-4\). Thus (3) holds for all \(n\geq3\).

We will also need positivity of the tails. In fact,
\[
R_k(n)\geq \frac{k^2-2k}{k-1} \qquad(2\leq k\leq n-1). \tag{9}
\]
This follows by backward induction. At \(k=n-1\), it is an immediate algebraic consequence of
\(R_{n-1}=n-1+n/4\) and \(n>2\). For the induction step, suppose
\[
R_{k+1}\geq\frac{(k+1)^2-2(k+1)}{k}
=\frac{k^2-1}{k}>0.
\]
Then \(R_{k+1}>0\), and the function \(y\mapsto k-(k+1)/y\) is increasing for positive \(y\). Hence
\[
R_k=k-\frac{k+1}{R_{k+1}}
\geq k-\frac{k(k+1)}{k^2-1}
=\frac{k(k-2)}{k-1},
\]
which is (9). In particular, \(R_3>0\), whenever that tail occurs, and \(R_2\geq0\). These facts will ensure below that the relevant continuants do not vanish and will determine their signs.

### 2. A suitable square root of 5 modulo \(p\)

Now let \(p\) be prime and suppose
\[
p\equiv1\pmod {10}\quad\text{or}\quad p\equiv9\pmod {10}. \tag{10}
\]
The small primes \(2,3,5,7\) do not satisfy (10), so
\[
p\geq11. \tag{11}
\]
In particular, \(p\) is odd and \(p\ne5\).

We claim that \(5\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(p\). By quadratic reciprocity, since \(5\equiv1\pmod4\),
\[
\left(\frac5p\right)=\left(\frac p5\right).
\]
Condition (10) implies \(p\equiv1\) or \(4\pmod5\). Both are nonzero squares modulo \(5\): \(1=1^2\) and \(4=2^2\). Thus
\((5/p)=1\), and there is an integer \(r\) such that
\[
r^2\equiv5\pmod p. \tag{12}
\]
Let \(x_1\) be the representative of \(r\) in \(\{0,1,\ldots,p-1\}\). It is nonzero, since otherwise (12) would imply \(p\mid5\), contrary to \(p\geq11\). Of the two roots \(x_1\) and \(p-x_1\), exactly one is even because \(p\) is odd. Define \(x\) to be that even root. Then
\[
0<x<p,\qquad x\equiv \pm r\pmod p,
\]
so
\[
x^2\equiv5\pmod p. \tag{13}
\]
Moreover,
\[
x\geq4. \tag{14}
\]
Indeed, if \(x\leq3\), then \(x^2\leq9<p\). Because \(5<p\), congruence (13) would then force the equality \(x^2=5\), which is impossible for an integer. Since \(x\) is positive and even, the only smaller possibility would in any event be \(x=2\).

Set
\[
n=x-1. \tag{15}
\]
By (14), \(n\geq3\), so this is a valid index of the sequence. Because of (13), there is a positive integer \(c\) such that
\[
x^2-5=pc. \tag{16}
\]
It is positive because \(x\geq4\). Also,
\[
c<n. \tag{17}
\]
Indeed, \(x<p\) implies \(p\geq x+1\), and hence
\[
pc=x^2-5<(x-1)(x+1)\leq(x-1)p=np.
\]
Cancelling the positive number \(p\) gives (17).

The integer \(c\) is odd. The number \(x\) is even, so \(x^2-5\) is odd. Equation (16) says that this odd number is \(pc\); as \(p\) is odd, \(c\) must also be odd. Consequently,
\[
\gcd(c,8)=1. \tag{18}
\]

By (3), (15), and (16),
\[
P_2=n^2+2n-4=(n+1)^2-5=x^2-5=pc. \tag{19}
\]
It remains to understand how much of this product cancels against \(P_3\) in \(R_2=P_2/P_3\).

### 3. The cofactor \(c\) cancels

We first prove
\[
c\mid P_3. \tag{20}
\]
By (17), \(1\leq c\leq n-1\), and therefore
\[
c\mid(n-1)!. \tag{21}
\]
Equation (7) can be rearranged as
\[
2P_3(n-2)=4(n-1)!-P_2T_n.
\]
Both terms on the right are divisible by \(c\), by (21) and (19). Thus
\[
c\mid 2P_3(n-2). \tag{22}
\]
There is a small issue that \(c\) need not be coprime to \(n-2\), so we remove that factor using (19). Since
\[
pc=P_2=n^2+2n-4=(n-2)(n+4)+4, \tag{23}
\]
multiply the number in (22) by \(n+4\). It follows that \(c\) divides
\[
2P_3(n-2)(n+4)=2P_3(pc-4).
\]
The term \(2P_3pc\) is itself divisible by \(c\), so subtraction shows that
\[
c\mid8P_3.
\]
By (18), Euclid's lemma now yields (20).

Write
\[
P_3=cd \tag{24}
\]
for an integer \(d\). This \(d\) is nonzero. For \(n=3\), one has \(P_3=P_n=4\). For \(n\geq4\), (9) gives \(R_3=P_3/P_4>0\), so in particular \(P_3\ne0\). Therefore, using (19), (24), and (2),
\[
R_2(n)=\frac{P_2}{P_3}=\frac{pc}{cd}=\frac pd. \tag{25}
\]
Furthermore,
\[
d>0. \tag{26}
\]
To see this, note first that \(P_2=pc>0\), and \(P_3\ne0\), so \(R_2=P_2/P_3\ne0\). The estimate (9) at \(k=2\) gives \(R_2\geq0\), and hence actually \(R_2>0\). Equation (25), together with \(p>0\), then forces \(d>0\).

### 4. The prime \(p\) does not cancel

We next prove
\[
p\nmid d. \tag{27}
\]
Suppose instead that \(p\mid d\). Then (24) implies \(p\mid P_3\), while (19) gives \(p\mid P_2\).

We propagate these two divisibilities along the continuant recurrence. Suppose for some \(j\), with \(2\leq j<n-1\), that \(p\mid P_j\) and \(p\mid P_{j+1}\). From (1),
\[
(j+1)P_{j+2}=jP_{j+1}-P_j,
\]
so \(p\mid(j+1)P_{j+2}\). But \(j+1\leq n-1<p\), because \(n=x-1<x<p\). Since \(p\) is prime, it cannot divide the positive integer \(j+1\). Euclid's lemma therefore gives \(p\mid P_{j+2}\). Starting from \(P_2,P_3\), induction yields \(p\mid P_n\). Yet \(P_n=4\), which is impossible because \(p\geq11\). This contradiction proves (27).

Since \(p\) is prime, (27) says precisely that
\[
\gcd(p,d)=1. \tag{28}
\]
Combining (25), (26), and (28), the fraction \(p/d\) is already in lowest terms with positive denominator. Hence the reduced numerator of \(R_2(n)\) is exactly \(p\).

Finally, the original continued fraction is \(C_n=1/R_2(n)\). Thus if \(R_2(n)=p/d\) in lowest terms, then
\[
C_n=\frac d p
\]
is also in lowest terms, and its reduced denominator is \(p\). Therefore
\[
a(n)=p
\]
for the index \(n=x-1\) constructed above. This proves that every prime congruent to \(1\) or \(9\) modulo \(10\) occurs in A363347.
